title: Typing | Fun Facts: The Natural World
description: This course is for the continued development of typing skills for students who have already mastered touch typing basics. Students will type and discover fun facts relating to animals, pets, dinosaurs, marine life, outer space and more in 200 lessons.

lessons.name: Amazing Animals Introduction
lessons.text1: Amazing animals exist all over the world. Let's learn about some spectacular species while practicing our typing skills.

lessons.name: Tigers
lessons.text1: Tigers have striped skin just like their fur. Also, no two tiger stripes are the same! Each tiger has its own unique pattern.

lessons.name: Reindeer
lessons.text1: A reindeer's eyeballs turn from golden in the summer to blue every winter! Why? Blue eyes help them see at lower light levels during the long winter. Reindeer are unique this way!

lessons.name: Sloths
lessons.text1: Did you know that sloths are good swimmers? Sometimes, they drop down into the water from a treetop perch and use their long arms to swim! They are especially good at the backstroke.

lessons.name: Cows
lessons.text1: Cows have best friends. When a cow has her preferred companion cow next to her, she shows fewer signs of stress as measured by her heart rate than when she has a random other cow next to her.

lessons.name: Brown Bat
lessons.text1: The little brown bat is one of the sleepiest animals on Earth. It sleeps about 19.9 hours a day. The mammal that sleeps the least is the African bush elephant, which sleeps only about 2 hours a day total.

lessons.name: Horse
lessons.text1: Have you ever seen a horse make a funny expression? Turns out, horses use their facial expressions as a form of communication with other horses! So far, we've identified around 17 different facial movements.

lessons.name: Hamster
lessons.text1: A pet hamster can run up to 5 miles a night on a hamster wheel. Why? In the wild, hamsters scurry through complex underground burrowing systems. Jumping on the wheel helps hamsters mimic this natural behavior.

lessons.name: Polar Bears
lessons.text1: Polar bears ask to share food by touching noses. One polar bear will slowly circle and approach another bear who is feeding. They then touch their nose to the nose of the feeding bear to ask if they can have some, too.

lessons.name: Amazing Animals Game 1
lessons.text1: sloth tiger pattern horse facial hamster reindeer blue polar bear brown bat cow

lessons.name: Giant Pandas
lessons.text1: Most giant pandas on Earth are owned by China. Zoos that want to keep pandas internationally must pay the Chinese government about a million dollars a year to rent them. As of 2023, 56 pandas were on loan to other countries.

lessons.name: Hummingbird Wings
lessons.text1: Unlike other bird species, hummingbirds can fly backwards. While hovering in the air, hummingbird wings can beat from 720 to 5,400 times per minute. That's a lot of energy! After flying, hummingbirds spend most of their time resting on branches to recover.

lessons.name: Armadillo
lessons.text1: Armadillos swallow air to make themselves float as they swim. They can also exhale air to make themselves sink and walk along the bottom of a body of water using their sharp claws to dig into the ground. Plus, they can hold their breath for 6 whole minutes!

lessons.name: Cat Island
lessons.text1: There are many islands in Japan that have significantly more cats than humans. They attract tons of locals and tourists! These islands are called nekojimas or "cat islands." Japan is also home to the island of Okunoshima, which is full of rabbits, and a fabulous fox village in the city of Shiroishi!

lessons.name: Bumblebee Bat
lessons.text1: One of the world's smallest mammals is the bumblebee bat, also known as the Kitti's hog-nosed bat. It is found in Thailand and Myanmar and weighs less than a penny, making it smaller than some insects. Despite its size, the bumblebee bat is an agile hunter, using echolocation to locate and catch insects.

lessons.name: Kangaroo
lessons.text1: Kangaroos are the only large animals that primarily use hopping as their means of locomotion. Their hind legs are powerful and adapted for hopping, allowing them to cover close to 30 feet in a single leap and reach speeds of 40 mph. When walking slowly, they use their tail as a "fifth leg" for support and balance!

lessons.name: Mirror Test
lessons.text1: Did you know elephants can recognize themselves in mirrors? They're some of the few animals besides humans and some great apes to pass the "mirror test." Researchers have found that elephants have a strong sense of self-awareness and can even use their trunks to touch the parts of their bodies reflected in the mirror.

lessons.name: Fingerprints
lessons.text1: Did you know the fingerprints of koalas are similar to those of humans? Biological anthropologist Maciej Henneberg discovered that koala fingerprints have loops, whirls, and ridges almost identical to ours. Luckily for detectives, Henneberg stated it is "extremely unlikely that koala prints would be found at the scene of a crime."

lessons.name: Energy
lessons.text1: Sloths are known for their slow movements and sleepy demeanor, but did you know they're also known for another unusual habit? They only defecate once a week, and almost always on the ground! For sloths, it takes an enormous amount of time and energy to digest their food; it takes them a whole month to digest only one leaf!

lessons.text1: giant panda armadillo cat island bumblebee bat kangaroo locomotion elephant sloth koala fingerprint

lessons.name: Under the Sea Introduction
lessons.text1: What kinds of creatures lurk under the sea? Practice your typing skills while discovering cool facts about marine life.

lessons.name: Blue
lessons.text1: The ocean looks blue because water absorbs the red colors in the color spectrum and reflects blue.

lessons.name: Whale Shark
lessons.text1: The largest fish in the world is a shark! The whale shark can grow longer than 50 feet and weigh several tons.

lessons.name: Whiskers
lessons.text1: What do cats and seals have in common? Whiskers! Both cats and seals use their whiskers to hunt their prey.

lessons.name: Coral Reef
lessons.text1: Did you know that there are bustling cities under the sea? They're called coral reefs, and they are home to more than 25% of marine life despite only taking up less than 1% of the ocean floor.

lessons.name: Oxygen
lessons.text1: Would you have guessed that most of the Earth's oxygen comes from water? Oceanic plankton perform photosynthesis, generating about 50-80% of Earth's oxygen. These tiny plankton are vital to our survival!

lessons.name: Sharks vs. Orcas
lessons.text1: Great white sharks are extremely afraid of orcas, also called killer whales. Great whites will avoid areas where they've seen or passed by an orca for up to a year, even if it's within their normal hunting grounds.

lessons.name: Ancient Sharks
lessons.text1: There were sharks on Earth before there were trees! Sharks have been on our planet for over 400 million years, while the first tree came along about 350 million years ago. Some species of shark have changed very little over this large span of time.

lessons.name: Deep Sea
lessons.text1: Have you ever seen an animal glow in the dark? Bioluminescence is a phenomenon in which living organisms produce their own light through a chemical reaction in their cells. Deep sea creatures such as the anglerfish, sea salp, squid, and jellyfish are bioluminescent.

lessons.name: Under the Sea Game 1
lessons.text1: spectrum shark whiskers seals coral life photosynthesis whale ancient bioluminescence

lessons.name: Blobfish
lessons.text1: The blobfish was voted the "World's Ugliest Animal" in 2013. The blobfish is a deep-sea creature that lives between 2,000 and 4,000 feet beneath the surface, where the pressure is 120 times greater than at sea level. It has no skeleton or muscle, but it does have an unusual face!

lessons.name: Mimic Octopus
lessons.text1: The mimic octopus is known for its ability to mimic the appearance and behavior of other animals, such as lionfish, sea snakes, jellyfish, crabs, and more! It can contort its body to resemble other creatures and change the color and texture of its skin to blend in with its surroundings.

lessons.name: Dolphins
lessons.text1: Dolphins need to sleep, but their sleep looks a little different than ours! Dolphins only shut half their brain off when getting shut eye. The other half stays at a low level of alertness to protect against predators, obstacles, or other animals. They also must stay conscious in order to breathe.

lessons.name: Jellyfish Lake
lessons.text1: Have you ever wanted to swim with jellyfish? Normally, that would be really dangerous. But if you visit Jellyfish Lake in Palau, you can swim with millions of golden jellyfish! Golden jellyfish don't have stingers, so it's a lot safer to swim alongside them. They migrate across the lake every day!

lessons.name: Gills
lessons.text1: Fish don't have lungs, so they can't breathe air or sneeze. But did you know they can cough? If foreign particles get caught in their gills, they can push water through their gills to dislodge or expel the particles. This process is similar to how a human will cough if something gets caught in their throat!

lessons.name: Three Hearts
lessons.text1: Did you know that octopuses have three hearts and blue blood? Two of its hearts are in charge of moving blood past its gills, while the third is in charge of circulation. Octopuses can also change color and texture to blend in with their surroundings, spray ink on their enemies, and even regenerate lost limbs.

lessons.name: Immortal
lessons.text1: There is a species of jellyfish that can theoretically live forever! When faced with stress or damage, the immortal jellyfish can revert to its juvenile form, a process known as transdifferentiation. While it can be killed by predators or disease, it has the potential to live indefinitely under ideal conditions.

lessons.name: Sea Sponge
lessons.text1: Have you ever seen a sea sponge? You might think they are plants, but they are actually animals! Sea sponges are considered the "least evolutionarily advanced" animal on the planet. However, they are more than ancient! They evolved 500 million years ago and continued to live through extinction events.

lessons.name: Blue Whale
lessons.text1: Blue whales are the largest animals on Earth, with some growing up to 30 meters long and weighing as much as 130,000 kilograms. Their tongues alone can weigh as much as an elephant, and their calls are the loudest of any other creature! Unfortunately, due to hunting, they are now classified as an endangered species.

lessons.name: Baby Animals Introduction
lessons.text1: Baby animals have unique traits and behaviors that make their early life special. Let's practice typing to uncover some amazing information!

lessons.name: Panda Cub
lessons.text1: When a panda bear is born, the cub is only four ounces. That's smaller than a mouse!

lessons.name: Quills
lessons.text1: Baby porcupines are born with a full set of quills that are soft at birth but harden within an hour.

lessons.name: Litter
lessons.text1: The world record for kittens born in a single litter is 19! However, dogs have cats beat. The world record for puppies born in a litter is 24!

lessons.name: Joey
lessons.text1: A baby kangaroo, or joey, is so tiny when born that it's only about the size of a lima bean. It stays in its mom's pouch until it grows big enough to explore.

lessons.name: Roar
lessons.text1: Baby lions, also called cubs, can't roar when they're born. It takes them several months of practice to master the big, powerful roar that adult lions are known for.

lessons.name: Puppies
lessons.text1: Baby dogs, or puppies, are born with no teeth at all! Their baby teeth start to come in around three weeks old, and they'll start chewing on things to help them grow.

lessons.name: Teaspoon
lessons.text1: Newborn hummingbirds are incredibly small and can fit into a teaspoon. They are 1 inch long when they hatch. They grow quickly and learn to hover and fly in just a few weeks.

lessons.name: Kittens
lessons.text1: Baby cats, or kittens, are born with their eyes closed. They can't see anything for the first couple of weeks. They rely on their other senses to navigate and find their mom for food.

lessons.name: Baby Animals Game 1
lessons.text1: cub kitten puppy armadillo kangaroo hummingbird newborn porcupine

lessons.name: Armadillo
lessons.text1: Most baby armadillos are born in a group of four, all of the same gender. This happens because armadillos usually give birth to identical quadruplets from a single fertilized egg, which splits into four embryos.

lessons.name: Seahorse
lessons.text1: Seahorse babies are called fry. They are born from their father's pouch. They are extremely tiny, often just a few millimeters long. They are fully independent from birth and float with the currents to avoid predators.

lessons.name: Eggs
lessons.text1: Some reptiles, like alligators, crocodiles, and sea turtles, lay their eggs in the sand. The temperature of the sand determines the gender of the hatchling. Cooler sand produces more males and warmer sand produces more females.

lessons.name: Chrysalis
lessons.text1: Baby butterflies start as caterpillars. Over the course of about 2 weeks, they undergo a complete transformation called metamorphosis. They create a chrysalis around themselves. This is where the caterpillar transforms into a butterfly.

lessons.name: Hatch
lessons.text1: Baby sea turtles hatch from their eggs on the beach at night. They instinctively head toward the ocean's reflection of the moon, which guides them to the water. There are about 80-100 hatchlings per nest, and they all hatch at the same time.

lessons.name: Egg Tooth
lessons.text1: Baby animals that hatch from eggs have a special egg tooth to help them break free from their egg. Baby crocodiles, alligators, snakes, turtles, and birds are a few examples. This special egg tooth will disappear a few days after they hatch.

lessons.name: Otter
lessons.text1: Baby otters, or pups, are born on land and can't swim immediately. They learn how to swim and hunt for food from their mothers. They often hold hands with each other or with their mothers while floating on the water. This helps them stay together and not drift apart.

lessons.name: Ducklings
lessons.text1: Ducklings are very cute with their fluffy yellow feathers! When they're young, they rely on their mothers for warmth and protection. They can't swim right away. As they grow, their feathers develop, and they learn how to swim. The transition from fuzzy baby to a fully feathered duck is an important part of their development.

lessons.name: Giraffe
lessons.text1: Unlike other mammals who typically lie down during labor, female giraffes give birth while standing up! This means that the newborn falls about 6 feet to the ground. Surprisingly, the fall doesn't harm the calf. Within just 30 minutes of being born, the calf can stand up on its own and start walking!

lessons.name: Nature Introduction
lessons.text1: The natural world is full of unbelievable phenomena and mysteries. Let's learn more about nature together as we level up our typing skills!

lessons.name: Bamboo
lessons.text1: Bamboo is the fastest growing grass! It can grow up to 35 inches in one day and can reach maturity in just 90 days.

lessons.name: Cell Reception
lessons.text1: Need to make a call after climbing the tallest mountain in the world? Good news! Although the peak is remote, there is cell reception at the top of Mount Everest!

lessons.name: Talking Trees
lessons.text1: Can trees talk? There is evidence that shows that trees can communicate with each other using a network of fungi. Roots connect to the fungi and the fungi sends signals to other parts of the forest!

lessons.name: Fungus
lessons.text1: The largest living organism in the world is a fungus. The giant Armillaria ostoyae grows in the soil of Oregon's Blue Mountains, covering 2,200 acres in total. It's at least 2,400 years old but could be as old as 8,650 years!

lessons.name: Africa
lessons.text1: There is only one continent that spans all four hemispheres. Africa touches the Northern, Southern, Eastern, and Western Hemispheres. Therefore, Africa is the only continent with land crossed by both the prime meridian and the equator.

lessons.name: Sphere
lessons.text1: Modern GPS allows scientists to measure Earth down to the centimeter. What they've discovered is that while Earth is a sphere, it is not a perfect sphere. Due to its fast rotation, Earth is slightly flattened at both the North and South poles.

lessons.name: First Sunrise
lessons.text1: Want to greet the sun before everyone else? You can be the first person to see the sunrise every day on the East Cape in New Zealand! Want to be the first of the first? Head to the peak of Maunga Hikurangi, which is the highest non-volcanic peak of the North Island.

lessons.name: Mauna Loa
lessons.text1: Hawaii's Mauna Loa is the largest active volcano in the world. Its name means "long mountain" in Hawaiian, and it rises 30,000 feet above the seafloor, which is a greater height than Mt. Everest! Scientists have noted that the seafloor actually bends underneath the weight of Mauna Loa.

lessons.name: Nature Game 1
lessons.text1: bamboo grass Everest roots organism fungus continent hemisphere sphere sunrise volcano

lessons.name: Hemisphere
lessons.text1: Of all of the world's human population, about ninety percent dwell in the Northern Hemisphere. That's 6.4 billion people! The Northern Hemisphere is the half of the world above the equator, and the Southern Hemisphere is below the equator.

lessons.name: Largest Flower
lessons.text1: The biggest flower in the world is the Rafflesia arnoldii, from the rainforests of Indonesia. It can grow up to three feet in diameter and weigh up to 15 pounds! The Rafflesia arnoldii is also known for its foul odor, which is similar to rotting meat and attracts insects for pollination.

lessons.name: Sahara
lessons.text1: Did you know the Sahara used to be a lush garden full of animals and green plants? Scientists think it will be green again in about 10,000 to 15,000 years! This switch from desert to grassland is caused by the Earth's rotation around its axis, and the pattern repeats roughly every 23,000 years.

lessons.name: Atacama
lessons.text1: The driest non polar desert in the world is the Atacama Desert, which is located on the Pacific coast of South America. The desert is so dry that evidence shows it likely didn't experience significant rainfall for a period of about 400 years. NASA has even used it as a testing ground for Mars rovers!

lessons.name: Rings
lessons.text1: You can tell how old a tree is by counting its rings. But is it possible to tell how old a fish is? Yes! You can count the rings on its ear bone. Each ring is equal to one year of growth! Sometimes, you can also determine a fish's age by counting the ridges on its scales, though that can be less accurate.

lessons.name: Lightning
lessons.text1: Can you guess how many lightning strikes occur each day around the world? 8.6 million! That's about 100 lightning strikes every second. Each lightning flash contains between 100 million and 1 billion volts of electricity. You could light a standard light bulb for 3 months with an average bolt of lightning!

lessons.name: Temperature
lessons.text1: What do you think is hotter, the surface of the sun or a bolt of lightning? While a bolt of lightning technically can't have a temperature, it does heat the air around it. The temperature of the air around a bolt of lightning can be 50,000 degrees Fahrenheit, which is five times hotter than the surface of the sun.

lessons.name: Hyperion
lessons.text1: The tallest tree in the world is a redwood tree named Hyperion, located in California's Redwood National Park. It stands at over 379 feet tall and is currently off-limits to tourists to protect the surrounding forests. Those who leave designated trails to find Hyperion could be faced with a $5,000 fine or up to six months in jail.

lessons.name: Gold
lessons.text1: Did you know that the ocean contains more than 20 million tons of gold? Unfortunately, the concentration is so low that it would take an enormous amount of seawater to produce even tiny gold particles. Several people throughout history have claimed they can extract gold from seawater more efficiently, but these claims have all been hoaxes!

lessons.name: Daring Dinos Introduction
lessons.text1: Dinosaurs have fascinated us for centuries. How many can you name? Learn about these daring dinos while improving your typing speed and accuracy!

lessons.name: Velociraptor
lessons.text1: Velociraptors were small turkey-sized creatures. These daring dinos may have had feathers and hunted in coordinated packs.

lessons.name: Argentinosaurus
lessons.text1: Argentinosaurus was a giant herbivorous sauropod, reaching up to 100 feet long and weighing 100 tons, making it one of the largest dinosaurs ever.

lessons.name: Ichthyosaur
lessons.text1: Ichthyosaurs, with their sleek snouts and paddle-like arms and legs, ruled the oceans. These dinos helped shape the marine ecosystem before becoming extinct in the late Cretaceous period.

lessons.name: Stegosaurus
lessons.text1: The Stegosaurus was an impressive Jurassic herbivore roaming the Mesozoic era around 150 million years ago. Known for its large back plates, it also featured a thagomizer, a spiked tail used to defend against predators.

lessons.name: Pterodactyl
lessons.text1: Pterodactyls were the first flying vertebrates, soaring during the late Jurassic and early Cretaceous periods. Like birds, they had lightweight hollow bones. Like bats, their wings were made of elongated fingers connected by skin membranes.

lessons.name: Saltasaurus
lessons.text1: Saltasaurus was a sauropod with a giraffe-like neck. As herbivores, they ate low-lying vegetation and had whip-like tails with bony knobs for defense. They probably lived in herds, traveling as a pack to protect themselves against predators.

lessons.name: Protoceratops
lessons.text1: Protoceratops were small but feisty herbivores. They roamed the cold deserts in Mongolia in the late Cretaceous period. Protoceratops had a beak-like mouth and a distinctive tail with frills. They lacked the horns seen in larger relatives like Triceratops.

lessons.name: Ankylosaurus
lessons.text1: Ankylosaurus looked like a giant ship with a wide, heavily armored body covered with bony plates. Standing about 5.6 feet tall and weighing 8,000 kilograms, it had a tail that was about 2 feet long and weighed 20 kilograms. This was used to defend against predators.

lessons.name: Daring Dinos Game 1
lessons.text1: Velociraptor Argentinosaurus Ichthyosaurs Pterodactyls Stegosaurus Saltasaurus Protoceratops Ankylosaurus

lessons.name: Triceratops
lessons.text1: The word Triceratops means "three-horned face." These herbivores were huge and had a neck with frills and horns for defense.

lessons.name: Oculudentavis
lessons.text1: Oculudentavis is thought to have been the smallest dinosaur because of its bird-like features. It showed lizard traits like fused teeth, unique skull bones, and scaly skin.

lessons.name: Amphicoelias
lessons.text1: Amphicoelias altus was an 80-foot-long, 50-ton sauropod. This plant-eater was possibly the largest dinosaur, but scientists only have one huge vertebra to base their guesses on.

lessons.name: Diplodocus
lessons.text1: The Diplodocus had narrow, pointed, bony spines on its back. It used its long neck to reach food and drink water. Ligaments from its hip to neck held it horizontally without muscles.

lessons.name: Tyrannosaurus
lessons.text1: The Tyrannosaurus rex is probably the most famous of the dinosaurs. New studies show that their teeth were likely covered by lips, making them less scary than often depicted in movies.

lessons.name: Coelophysis
lessons.text1: Early carnivores like the Coelophysis used speed and sharp claws to hunt insects and small reptiles. Fossils indicate they may have practiced cannibalism, but newer analysis shows this is false.

lessons.name: Dromiceiomimus
lessons.text1: The Dromiceiomimus was one of the fastest dinosaurs, reaching 50 miles per hour. It had long legs, large eyes, and toothless jaws. This omnivore was originally classified as Struthiomimus, but it was redefined as its own genus in the 1970s.

lessons.name: Mamenchisaurus
lessons.text1: The Mamenchisaurus roamed the Asian forests and plains in the Late Jurassic period. This herbivorous sauropod reached up to 115 feet and 75 tons. It had an exceptionally long neck with 19 vertebrae and a whip-like tail. It likely swept its neck low to feed on shrubs.

lessons.name: Micropachycephalosaurus
lessons.text1: Micropachycephalosaurus, meaning "micro thick-headed lizard," was a tiny herbivorous ceratopsian from the Late Cretaceous period. Measuring around two meters, it had a thick, flattened skull, large eyes, and a short snout. Scientists think it may have used its skull for head-butting to establish dominance.

lessons.name: Outer Space Introduction
lessons.text1: Let's launch into the mysteries of the stars and planets with these fun facts guaranteed to blow your mind. Let's practice some typing skills while we're at it!

lessons.name: Space Height
lessons.text1: What's your space height? Astronauts typically get three percent taller on space missions! They return to their normal height once back on Earth.

lessons.name: Blood Moon
lessons.text1: What do you think a "blood moon" is? It's nothing too gruesome! During a lunar eclipse, light is bent in the Earth's atmosphere. This casts a reddish glow on the moon!

lessons.name: Europa
lessons.text1: Ever wonder if there is life out in space? Jupiter's moon Europa has water beneath its icy exterior. Why is this special? Water means there is the possibility of alien life!

lessons.name: Jupiter
lessons.text1: The Great Red Spot on Jupiter is actually a massive storm that's been raging on for 300 years. Now, the storm is starting to shrink! It could disappear entirely in the next few centuries.

lessons.name: Mars
lessons.text1: Why does Mars have a reddish color? The iron in the rocks and regolith (Martian soil) oxidizes, resulting in rust. Martian dust blows into the atmosphere, making the planet appear red from afar.

lessons.name: Fruit Flies
lessons.text1: What living things were the first to visit outer space? Fruit flies! The first batch of flies were sent into space in 1946 but never returned to Earth. In 1947, fruit flies were sent to space and safely recovered!

lessons.name: Venus
lessons.text1: On Venus, it snows metal. Venus is a hot planet, but there are snowcapped peaks beneath thick layers of clouds. The "snow" is actually two types of metal: galena and bismuthinite. It looks a little like shiny, metallic frost!

lessons.name: Gasses
lessons.text1: Want to walk on another planet? Only some are eligible. Even if we could get there, it wouldn't be possible to walk on planets like Jupiter, Neptune, Saturn, or Uranus, as they don't have a solid surface and are made mostly of gasses.

lessons.name: Outer Space Game 1
lessons.text1: space height blood moon Europa Jupiter Martian dust flies rocket flight Venus metallic frost gasses Neptune Saturn

lessons.name: Atmosphere
lessons.text1: Outer space is completely silent. Why? There is no atmosphere, which means no atoms and molecules. Sound is carried by atoms and molecules, so without them, there is nothing to carry it over distance. Without sound, there is also no echo.

lessons.name: Sunsets
lessons.text1: Martian dust creates unique sunsets! Sunsets on Mars are blue, not the yellow or orange colors that we are used to on Earth. The dust on Mars is made of very fine particles that allow more blue light to filter through as the sun goes down.

lessons.name: Olympus Mons
lessons.text1: The largest volcano in the solar system is on Mars. It is called Olympus Mons and is about three times as high as Mount Everest. Olympus Mons isn't a typical volcano. It's a shield volcano! Lava gently flows down its sides, making Olympus Mons wide and low in appearance.

lessons.name: Star Power
lessons.text1: There are more trees on Earth than stars in our galaxy. While the Milky Way has 100-400 billion stars, Earth has about three trillion trees! However, in the entire universe, astronomers have estimated approximately 200 billion trillion stars in what we can observe. That's a lot of star power!

lessons.name: Sun
lessons.text1: The Sun's radius is 432,690 miles. 109 Earths, lined up, would fit across the face of the Sun. It's so big that one million Earths could fit inside it if they were all squished together! But compared to other stars, our Sun isn't that big. The red giant, Betelgeuse, is about 700 times larger.

lessons.name: Moonquakes
lessons.text1: You've heard of earthquakes, but did you know they can happen on the moon? When that happens, it's called a moonquake! Moonquakes aren't as intense as earthquakes, but sometimes, they can last much longer. Earthquakes usually only last 10-30 seconds, but moonquakes sometimes last for over 10 minutes!

lessons.name: Astronauts
lessons.text1: Astronauts in space exercise for at least 2.5 hours every day to prevent their muscles and bones from deteriorating or atrophying due to the lack of gravity. They use treadmills, bicycles, or weight-lifting machines that have been modified in creative ways to make them possible to use with no gravity!

lessons.name: Neutron Star
lessons.text1: Did you know that just one teaspoon of matter from a neutron star would weigh more than one billion tons? Neutron stars are incredibly dense collapsed cores of massive stars that have exploded in supernovae. Despite being only about 12 miles in diameter, a neutron star is even more dense than our Sun!

lessons.name: Diamond Planet
lessons.text1: Forty light-years away, there is a planet covered in diamonds called 55 Cancri e. It's twice the size of Earth and eight times its mass. It's estimated that about a third of the planet is made up of pure diamond. Called a super-Earth because of its large radius, this diamond planet is rich in carbon where Earth is rich in oxygen.

lessons.name: Groups of Animals Introduction
lessons.text1: A collective noun is a term that describes a specific group. There are a lot of fun collective nouns for groups of animals. Let's practice typing some of these animal group names together!

lessons.name: School
lessons.text1: One fish is called a fish. Many fish are called fish. A group of fish is called a school! Pretty smart, don't you think?

lessons.name: Cauldron
lessons.text1: A group of bats is called a cauldron. These furry, fluttering creatures can also be called a colony!

lessons.name: Flock
lessons.text1: A group of sheep is called a flock. A farmer can have a flock of 2 sheep or a flock of 1,500 or more sheep! That's a very large flock!

lessons.name: Prickle
lessons.text1: Porcupines are known for their pointy and sharp quills that stick out of their bodies. But did you know that a group of porcupines is called a prickle?

lessons.name: Cackling
lessons.text1: Hyenas are known for their cackling "laugh." So it makes sense that a group of hyenas is sometimes referred to as a cackle! They can also be called a clan.

lessons.name: Rhumba
lessons.text1: Have you ever seen a rhumba? Not sure what that is? Well, it's a group of rattlesnakes! You should probably stay away from a rhumba if you ever come across one!

lessons.name: Colony
lessons.text1: A group of ants is called a colony. They can also be referred to as an army! Ants build extensive tunnel systems underground. At the center of it all lives their queen!

lessons.name: Swarm
lessons.text1: A group of bees is called a swarm. They build their home in a hive, where their queen also lives. When bees feel threatened, they will all gather together and swarm their predator!

lessons.name: Groups of Animals Game 1
lessons.text1: fish bats sheep porcupines hyena rattlesnake ants bees hive quills

lessons.name: Pod
lessons.text1: A group of whales is called a pod. That's the name for a group of dolphins, too! These underwater mammals will hunt together, swim together, and protect each other while in their pod.

lessons.name: Litter
lessons.text1: A group of cats is called a clowder. A group of kittens is called a cluster. But a group of kittens living with their mother is called a litter. So many different names for a group of furry felines!

lessons.name: Congregation
lessons.text1: Even though alligators and crocodiles look similar, they are not the same, and neither are their group names! A group of alligators is called a congregation. A group of crocodiles is called a bask.

lessons.name: Raft
lessons.text1: Have you ever seen a group of otters? Have you ever seen them floating on their backs in the water? Funny, because when they are in a group, they are known as a raft! They can also be known as a family. How sweet!

lessons.name: Pack
lessons.text1: A group of dogs can have different names. A group of puppies with the same mother is called a litter. A group of dogs is often called a pack, especially if they are hunting. Another general term for a group of dogs is a kennel.

lessons.name: Gaggle
lessons.text1: A group of geese is called a gaggle when it is on land. A group of geese is called a flock when it is flying. Did you know that a goose chooses one mate for its entire life? A female goose is called a goose, but a male goose is called a gander.

lessons.name: Thunder
lessons.text1: A hippopotamus is often nicknamed a hippo. When referring to them in the plural form, they are called hippopotami or hippopotamuses. When referring to a group of them, they are called a bloat or a thunder! They sure do have a tongue-twisting name! How easily did you type their name?

lessons.name: Flamboyance
lessons.text1: A group of flamingos is called a flamboyance. These social birds are known for their bright pink feathers and are mainly found in parts of Africa, South America, and the Caribbean. Their unique pink coloring comes from the carotenoids found in their food, particularly algae and brine shrimp.

lessons.name: Herd
lessons.text1: A group of elephants is called a herd, but it can also be called a parade! Herds vary in size, but they are multigenerational and matriarchal. A typical herd is led by one female elephant matriarch. This matriarch is usually the oldest in the group. She unofficially leads the herd, which generally consists of most of her offspring and her offsprings' offspring.

lessons.name: Professional Pets Introduction
lessons.text1: Have you ever heard of a pet with a job? From therapy dogs to museum curators, animals have been helping humans out for years. Level up your typing skills while learning about these professional pets.

lessons.name: Military
lessons.text1: Did you know that some dolphins work for the navy? Dolphins are trained to locate underwater mines that could pose a risk to civilian or military ships.

lessons.name: Landscapers
lessons.text1: Is your yard full of weeds? Consider hiring a herd of goats! Goats make great weed eaters. Riverside Park in New York City hires goats annually as landscapers!

lessons.name: Magic
lessons.text1: Magic the miniature horse is a therapy horse who visits assisted living and rehab facilities. One patient hadn't spoken in three years until she laid eyes on Magic!

lessons.name: Therapy Dogs
lessons.text1: Have you ever wished you could have a job listening to stories? For some dogs, that's true! Reading therapy dogs encourage reluctant readers to improve their skills in a safe and comforting environment.

lessons.name: Animal Influencers
lessons.text1: Influencers aren't just human! Dogs, cats, and even foxes can gain influencer status. Grumpy Cat became known across the internet for her iconic scowl or "grumpy" expression, which was caused by an underbite and feline dwarfism.

lessons.name: Bosco
lessons.text1: Can you elect a dog for mayor? In Sunol, California, that's what they did! Resident Brad Leber put his dog, Bosco, on the ballot. Bosco won the election! Now, there is a special tavern that commemorates this unique elected official!

lessons.name: Sheepdogs
lessons.text1: Some dog breeds have a specific vocation! Sheepdogs have been bred to herd sheep. Different dogs will herd in different ways, but generally, herding involves collecting sheep together when they are dispersed and then herding them forward as a group.

lessons.name: Mousers
lessons.text1: Cats have had jobs for centuries! Felines traveled the world by ship alongside humans, employed as mousers to keep rodent populations under control. The oldest evidence of cats living alongside humans comes from a burial site in Cyprus, about 9,500 years ago!

lessons.name: Tama
lessons.text1: A cat named Tama was a train conductor in Japan! Her primary job was to greet passengers. Instead of money, Tama was compensated in cat food. She received a golden name tag noting her name and occupation. She also received a station master's cap, which took 6 months to make!

lessons.name: Leo
lessons.text1: Animals can be movie stars, too! From Toto in The Wizard of Oz to Buddy in Air Bud, dogs and other animals have a long history appearing on the silver screen. The most famous might be Leo the Lion, the mascot for Metro Goldwyn Mayer, whose roar appears before every MGM film.

lessons.name: Balto
lessons.text1: Sled dogs are trained to pull a sled over snow. In 1925, an especially heroic sled dog, Balto, led a team of dogs to Nome, Alaska, delivering life-saving diphtheria antitoxin through blizzard conditions. If you are ever in New York City, you can see Balto's statue in Central Park!

lessons.name: Dogs
lessons.text1: A dog's sense of smell is 10,000 to 100,000 times more sensitive than a human's. Not only can they sniff out bombs, but they can also warn owners of oncoming epileptic seizures, diseases, and more! Some dogs can even detect low blood sugar in diabetic patients before it becomes critical.

lessons.name: Larry
lessons.text1: Did you know Britain has a special cabinet position? It's called Chief Mouser, and only cats are up for the job! Mousers have been employed by the government since the 1500s. Today, a cat named Larry holds the title. You can sometimes spot this furry feline outside of Downing Street in London!

lessons.name: Cher Ami
lessons.text1: Pigeons helped deliver communications in the First World War. A pigeon called Cher Ami saved the 77th Battalion when they were trapped behind enemy lines. Cher Ami was shot down by German soldiers, but he didn't stop flying until his message was delivered. Despite his injuries, Cher Ami survived!

lessons.name: Juliana
lessons.text1: Juliana was a Great Dane who was awarded two Blue Cross medals. The Blue Cross is an animal welfare charity that recognizes animals who have shown exceptional bravery. Juliana received her first medal in 1941 when an incendiary bomb fell through the roof of her house. She urinated on the bomb, extinguishing the fire!

lessons.name: Sir Indiana Bones
lessons.text1: Sir Indiana Bones is a black cat who works at the Museum of Osteology, also known as Skulls Unlimited, in Oklahoma City, USA. He was adopted by the museum staff after they formed a "Kitty Committee" to obtain approval. He spends his days playing with bones and raising money for Moore Animal Shelter and Adoption Center!

lessons.name: Knighthood
lessons.text1: Did you know a king penguin named Nils Olav holds the rank of knighthood in the Norwegian Army? The tradition began in 1972 when a Norwegian lieutenant made him the official King's Guard mascot and gave him the rank of lance corporal. Since then, he has been promoted each time the King's Guard has returned to the Edinburgh Zoo.

lessons.name: Weird Weather Introduction
lessons.text1: Weather can come in all different forms. Sometimes, it can be good. Sometimes not. Let's practice your typing skills while learning about some weird weather occurrences!

lessons.name: Antarctica
lessons.text1: In Antarctica, snow can fall so hard and densely that you cannot see your hand right in front of your face!

lessons.name: Fog
lessons.text1: Because fog has a unique name, you might not realize that it's just a cloud that is touching the Earth's surface.

lessons.name: Fire Whirl
lessons.text1: A fire whirl is a whirlwind of flame or ash that occurs when intense heat combines with turbulent winds. It is also known as a fire tornado or a fire devil.

lessons.name: Raisins
lessons.text1: Raisins are dried up grapes. During the hottest months of 2003 in Europe, a heatwave turned grapes into raisins before they were even picked off of the vine!

lessons.name: Tsunamis
lessons.text1: Tsunamis can travel as fast as a jet plane, or over 500 mph, when traveling through the deep ocean. This means that they can travel across oceans in less than a day.

lessons.name: Hurricanes
lessons.text1: Hurricanes spin differently in the Northern Hemisphere and the Southern Hemisphere. Hurricanes spin counterclockwise in the north, and they spin clockwise in the south.

lessons.name: Dust Storms
lessons.text1: Dirt mixed with wind can make dust storms. When the wind is extreme enough, it can cause what is known as a black blizzard. There is so much dirt in the air that it becomes nearly impossible to see.

lessons.name: Drought
lessons.text1: Too much sunshine is not always good. Long periods without rain can cause droughts. During droughts, crops die. Crops provide food for people and animals. Dead crops lead to food shortages, and people can go hungry.

lessons.name: Weird Weather Game 1
lessons.text1: snow fog fire raisins ocean clockwise dirt sunshine

lessons.name: Mudslide
lessons.text1: A mudslide occurs when there is a lot of rain that soaks the ground, making it unstable. This causes mud to start slipping down the sides of mountains. It can even carry rocks, trees, and cars. Then it becomes a landslide!

lessons.name: Lightning
lessons.text1: Lightning strikes the Earth about 40 million times each year. This means lightning hits the ground roughly 76 times each minute! Luckily, the CDC explains that the odds of being struck each year are less than one in a million.

lessons.name: Jupiter
lessons.text1: Earth isn't the only place with weather. Other planets have weather, too! If you've ever seen a picture of Jupiter, you've probably noticed its Great Red Spot. That's actually a massive storm that has been going on for over 100 years.

lessons.name: Frost Fairs
lessons.text1: During the Great Frost of 1683-84, the Thames River in England was completely frozen for two months, with the ice reaching a thickness of 11 inches. This allowed people to hold "Frost Fairs" on the ice with shops, entertainment, and even animals walking across it!

lessons.name: Black Ice
lessons.text1: Black ice is a transparent coating of ice on a surface. It can make pavement extremely slippery. It's called "black ice" because it's difficult to see and blends in with the pavement, especially at night. It forms when it lightly rains during freezing temperatures.

lessons.name: Clouds
lessons.text1: How much do you think a typical cloud weighs? Scientists have determined that an average cloud weighs about 500,000 kilograms, or 1.1 million pounds. That's the weight of about 100 elephants! How can something so heavy stay above our heads? Dry air is denser than clouds, so clouds are buoyant.

lessons.name: Red Rain
lessons.text1: On July 25, 2001, Kerala, India experienced a phenomenon known as "red rain," where heavy downpours of rain appeared red in color. Scientists discovered that the 'red rain' was due to rainwater mixing with Trentepohlia, a type of orange algae that lives on trees. This caused the rain to appear to be red.

lessons.name: Cloud Types
lessons.text1: Look into the sky and you may see some clouds! But which type do you see? Clouds can be categorized into a number of different types, including cumulus, stratus, and cirrus. Cumulus are low, puffy clouds. Stratus are low and flat, similar to a fog. Cirrus are high and wispy streaks that are actually made from ice crystals!

lessons.name: Waterspout
lessons.text1: A waterspout is a rotating column of air that forms over water. It is similar to a tornado. It sucks up lake or ocean water along with fish or other creatures swimming in the water. They blow around in the vortex until the wind speed decreases enough to let them fall back to the water or ground, making it look like it's raining fish!

lessons.name: Interesting Insects Introduction
lessons.text1: There are many interesting insects that live on our Earth. Let's practice your typing skills while learning about what makes them so interesting.

lessons.name: Goliath
lessons.text1: The Goliath beetle is one of the largest insects in the world. It can weigh as much as a small apple. Despite its size, this beetle can still fly!

lessons.name: Fireflies
lessons.text1: Fireflies light up at night with a special glow! They use their flashing lights to communicate with each other. This glow is called bioluminescence.

lessons.name: Glasswing
lessons.text1: The glasswing butterfly has transparent wings, making it nearly invisible when it flies. This helps it hide from predators. Its see-through wings are delicate and beautiful!

lessons.name: Cicadas
lessons.text1: Cicadas are known for their loud buzzing sounds. They spend most of their lives underground as nymphs, sometimes for 13 to 17 years, before emerging as adults to sing and mate.

lessons.name: Hercules
lessons.text1: The Hercules beetle has a giant horn on its head, which it uses to fight other beetles. This beetle is also incredibly strong, capable of lifting objects 850 times its own weight!

lessons.name: Dragonflies
lessons.text1: Dragonflies are amazing flyers! They can fly in all directions, even backward. Dragonflies are also among the fastest insects, zipping through the air to catch prey, such as mosquitoes.

lessons.name: Fleas
lessons.text1: Fleas may be tiny, but they can jump very high: about 200 times their own body length! That's like a person jumping over a skyscraper! They use their strong legs to hop from place to place.

lessons.name: Trapdoor
lessons.text1: Trapdoor spiders create clever hiding places. They dig burrows in the ground and cover them with a "trapdoor" made of silk and dirt. When an insect walks by, the spider quickly jumps out to grab it.

lessons.text1: beetle firefly butterfly cicada dragonfly flea spider trapdoor insect

lessons.name: Stick Insects
lessons.text1: Stick insects are masters of disguise. They look just like twigs or branches. This helps them hide from predators. Some species can even sway like a twig in the wind to make their disguise even better.

lessons.name: Silkworms
lessons.text1: Silkworms may not look exciting, but they are very special because they create silk, a material used to make beautiful fabrics. The silk comes from the cocoons they spin as they prepare to become moths.

lessons.name: Leafcutter Ants
lessons.text1: Leafcutter ants are amazing builders! They cut pieces of leaves and carry them back to their underground nests. However, the leaves are not their food. They use the leaves to grow a special fungus that they eat.

lessons.name: Bombardier Beetle
lessons.text1: The bombardier beetle has a unique defense mechanism. When threatened, it sprays a hot, stinky liquid from its abdomen to scare off predators. This chemical spray can reach temperatures of nearly 100 degrees Celsius!

lessons.name: Praying Mantis
lessons.text1: The praying mantis looks like it's praying, but that is actually its hunting stance! It can turn its head almost all the way around to spot prey and has lightning-fast reflexes to catch its meals, like flies and other small insects.

lessons.name: Dung Beetles
lessons.text1: Dung beetles are strong and have a very important job. They help clean up the environment by rolling and burying animal poop, also known as dung. Some dung beetles can roll balls of dung that are 50 times heavier than their own bodies!

lessons.name: Ants
lessons.text1: Ants are super strong for their small size. They can carry things that are up to 50 times their own body weight! Ants are also great team players. They live in colonies where they work together to build tunnels, find food, and take care of their queen.

lessons.name: Honeybees
lessons.text1: Honeybees are incredible because they make honey. They collect nectar from flowers, break it down into simple sugars, and store it in the honeycomb. They also communicate with each other by doing a special "waggle dance" to show where the best flowers are.

lessons.name: Butterflies
lessons.text1: Butterflies start their lives as crawling caterpillars. They go through an amazing transformation called metamorphosis to become beautiful, colorful flying insects. One of the most famous is the monarch butterfly, known for its bright orange and black wings. Monarch butterflies migrate thousands of miles every year!
